name: Trax Records
description: Trax Records is a foundational Chicago house-music label, generally dated to a late-1984 founding by Larry Sherman with Jesse Saunders, with Vince Lawrence contributing design and signings — though CTL's house-music brief explicitly grades Trax's founding year and credits DISPUTED, and this record preserves that flag. Sherman's Musical Products pressing plant in Bridgeport, acquired in 1983, fed the label from 1984–85, making Trax part of a vertically connected Chicago production chain: plant, label, clubs, and WBMX radio. Its classic release run came in 1985–87. The label's legacy is contested as well as foundational: CTL's music red-team documents that the 1987 Trax pressing of "Your Love" credited Frankie Knuckles for what was Jamie Principle's song, a credit Principle alleged in 2014 was taken without his consent. Rachael Cain (Screamin' Rachael) took over and revived the label in 2006; Sherman died of heart failure on April 9, 2020, at age 70. name: The Warehouse
description: The Warehouse was a DJ-led dance club at 206 S. Jefferson Street in Chicago's West Loop, in a three-story loft building, and is the nightclub widely credited as the birthplace of house music. Promoter Robert Williams opened the club in 1977 and installed New York DJ Frankie Knuckles as resident DJ in March 1977; Knuckles's residency ran to 1982. The room drew a Black, Latino, and largely gay crowd, and CTL's venue research grades it as one of the first clubs where gay and straight, Black, Latinx, and white clubgoers shared a dance floor. The best-supported etymology of "house music" derives the term from this club's name — patrons sought "Warehouse music," and Williams billed events as "house" parties. The City of Chicago landmarked the building, with a period of significance of 1977–1982; after Knuckles's 1982 departure, Williams rebranded the venture as the Music Box with Ron Hardy as resident DJ. CTL's house-music brief is explicit that the club, the DJ practice, and the recorded genre are three separate births, and this record preserves that distinction rather than the lone-inventor myth.

name: The Jeffersons
description: The Jeffersons, created by Norman Lear as a spin-off of All in the Family, aired on CBS from January 18, 1975, to July 2, 1985 — eleven seasons, 253 episodes that moved George and Louise Jefferson from Archie Bunker's Queens neighborhood to a deluxe apartment on Manhattan's Upper East Side, on the strength of George's dry-cleaning chain. At its conclusion it was the longest-running sitcom with a predominantly Black cast, and it is still described as the longest-running Black comedy in network television history; it was CBS's third-longest-running sitcom when it ended. Its quiet revolutions were structural: George Jefferson was a Black businessman whose wealth was the premise rather than the punchline, and its ensemble included Tom and Helen Willis, cited as the first regularly appearing interracial married couple on American primetime television. It was the first Black sitcom after Sanford and Son to reach the Nielsen top five, and in 1981–82 the first to stand as television's top comedy for a season. 'Movin' on up' became the language's shorthand for Black arrival — the record preserves what the phrase cost and what it claimed.

description: Ten City is a Chicago house music group formed in 1987, its name derived from “intensity.” The group began as Ragtyme — vocalist Byron Stingily, keyboardist Byron Burke, and guitarist Herb Lawson — working with producer Marshall Jefferson. description: South Side community organization formed in 1960 (as the Temporary Woodlawn Organization) to fight displacement and racial discrimination in Woodlawn. Spokesman/president Rev. Arthur M. name: The Bop (Chicago)
description: Chicago's postwar Black partner dance, danced from the 1940s through the 1960s on the South and West Sides; the direct ancestor of Chicago Steppin'. The community keeps the lineage as one taxonomy: Boppers, Steppers, and Walkers — 'One Dance, One Love.'

name: Truevine Missionary Baptist Church
description: Historic Black congregation; its building at 6720 S Stewart Av is a designated Chicago Landmark (built 1892).

name: The Rolling Stones
description: British rock band whose early career ran through Chicago: recording at Chess Studios (June 1964; November 1964; May 1965) and covering Chicago blues compositions.

name: The Hacienda
description: Manchester nightclub launched in 1982 by New Order with Factory Records' Tony Wilson (1982-1997); one of the first British clubs to champion Chicago house music -- the documented Chicago-house conduit carried here, not the UK scene itself.

name: The House Sound of Chicago
description: The House Sound of Chicago is a seven-track compilation released in 1986 by D.J. International Records with London Records — the first European compilation promoting Chicago house music, and the first house compilation issued by the label. D.J. International had been founded in 1985 by Rocky Jones and Benji Espinoza. The compilation carried the new Chicago sound abroad through tracks including Steve "Silk" Hurley's "Jack Your Body," Farley "Jackmaster" Funk and Jesse Saunders' "Love Can't Turn Around," featuring Darryl Pandy, and Marshall Jefferson's "Move Your Body." It stands as the record that first packaged Chicago house music for European audiences.

name: The Caravans
description: The Caravans were founded by Albertina Walker in 1951 from members of the Robert Anderson Singers, becoming one of the most prominent gospel groups of the 1950s–60s. The group's fluctuating membership included James Cleveland, Bessie Griffin, Shirley Caesar, Dorothy Norwood, Inez Andrews, Loleatta Holloway, and Cassietta George.

name: The Gay Sisters
description: The Gay Sisters — Evelyn and Geraldine (gospel piano innovators) and Mildred (singer) — were key figures of gospel's Golden Age, recording from 1948 to 1973, playing the Apollo Theatre, and appearing with Mahalia Jackson and the Clara Ward Singers at the first all-gospel concert at Carnegie Hall in 1950.

name: Ter-Mar Studios / Chess Studios
aliases: Ter-Mar Recording Studio; Ter Mar Recordings; Chess Recording Studios (release-credit variant)
description: Chess's Chicago studio identity at 2120 S. Michigan Avenue -- Ter-Mar, named for Terry and Marshall Chess, the operating name from the 1958 Sheldon rename -- recording the core Chess blues and R&B catalog (Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf, Chuck Berry, Etta James) with in-house bassist/arranger Willie Dixon; release credits often read 'Chess Studios.' Kept separate from CTL-E-0177 (Chess Studios venue/site record); see conflict CTL-CFL-000120.

name: THING (zine)
description: THING was a Black queer Chicago zine/magazine published 1989–1993; ten issues founded by designer/writer Robert Ford with editors Trent Adkins and Lawrence Warren. First issued November 1989 as a 20-page photocopied zine from Ford's Chicago apartment under the tagline “She Knows Who She Is,” it documented ball, club, and house culture, platformed pioneers such as Frankie Knuckles, Larry Heard, Deee-Lite, and RuPaul, and carried uncompromising HIV/AIDS coverage. Publication ended with Ford's death in 1993; a 460-page anthology of all ten issues was released by Primary Information in February 2025.

name: Technics SL-1200 turntable
aliases: SL-1200; Tec 12's; Wheels of Steel; Ones & Twos
description: The Technics SL-1200 direct-drive turntable (introduced 1972) became the standard DJ instrument of Chicago house — the hardware basis of the Frankie Knuckles and Ron Hardy club sets. The 1200's pitch control and torque made beat-matching and extended blends physically possible, underwriting the Chicago DJ-as-producer practice.

name: Teenie Harris Archive (Carnegie Museum of Art)
description: The photographic archive of Pittsburgh Courier photographer Charles 'Teenie' Harris, held by the Carnegie Museum of Art: the visual record of a Black newspaper's 40-year run.

name: Telecommunications Act of 1996
description: The 1996 federal deregulatory law: the structural shock that consolidated Black radio/TV ownership and defined the modern survival landscape.

name: The Black Effect Podcast Network
description: Podcast network founded by Charlamagne Tha God as a joint venture with iHeartMedia in 2020; positioned as the largest podcast publisher for Black audiences.

name: The Crisis
description: Official magazine of the NAACP, founded 1910 by W. E. B. Du Bois; a crucible of the Harlem Renaissance; in continuous publication (now quarterly).

name: The Plug
description: Data-driven tech news outlet covering the Black innovation economy, founded by Sherrell Dorsey (April 2016); began as an early-morning newsletter, evolved into a data-driven platform, became the first Black data-driven tech news publication syndicated on the Bloomberg Terminal; acquired by ImpactAlpha in 2023.

name: TheGrio TV
description: Byron Allen's 24/7 broadcast network for Black audiences, built from Light TV.

name: Tom Joyner
description: Syndicated radio host ('the Fly Jock') whose nationally syndicated Tom Joyner Morning Show (1994-2019) reached 15+ million daily listeners at its peak.

name: Travis Montaque
description: Entrepreneur; founder of Holler and co-founder/CEO of Group Black until his 2024 departure.

name: TV One
description: National cable television network targeting adult Black viewers; wholly owned by Urban One. Sister network CLEO TV is a Black-women-focused offshoot.

name: The Baltimore Collection
description: The Baltimore Collection is a set of 53 photographs of Black sitters held by the University of Delaware Library, which received the photographs as a donation in 2001. The collection arrived as 'found objects': the photographs carry no photographers, no sitter names, no dates, and no provenance. Between 2017 and 2023, University of Delaware seminars — documented in the Library's 'Curating Hidden Collections & the Black Archive' project — worked to reconstruct the collection's metadata. CultureTechLens's CTL-DR-PRESERVE-001 research cites the Baltimore Collection as a documented orphan-collection case: an archive whose subjects cannot be found, used, or cited until cataloging reconstructs who they were.

name: Tivoli Theatre
description: Balaban & Katz movie palace at 63rd & Cottage Grove, Woodlawn. Opened February 16, 1921; 3,520 seats; Rapp and Rapp, French Baroque. First of the B&K "big three." R&B/jazz showcase in its late years. Closed September 19, 1963; demolished shortly after.

name: Tower Theatre
description: Neighborhood movie house at 1510 E. 63rd St, Woodlawn. Opened early 1926 with just under 3,000 seats; Italian Renaissance by Fridstein & Company for Lubliner & Trinz; acquired by Balaban & Katz in 1928. Closed sometime in the 1950s (exact dates unresolved); later demolished.

name: Teatro Tariakuri
description: Nonprofit Latino dance and theatre performing arts organization established in Chicago in 2004 (501(c)(3) July 2020). Theatre Co. founded by actress/director Karla Galvan; theater house and school at 3117 W 63rd St serving Marquette Park and surrounding communities with affordable performing-arts classes; presenter in the Destinos Chicago International Latino Theater Festival.

name: TEAM Englewood Community Academy
description: TEAM Englewood opened in the former Englewood High School building under Renaissance 2010; shrank to 76 students (~98% African-American); its students were consolidated with Harper, Hope, and Robeson into the new $85M Englewood STEM High School (6835 S. Normal Blvd.), which opened Sept 3, 2019.

name: Teamwork Englewood
description: Englewood community development organization at 815 W. 63rd St., Floor 2. Formed in 2003 (sponsored by Pullman Bank and Trust, LISC/Chicago, and local churches); became the LISC New Communities Program lead agency for Englewood; publishes the Englewood Quality of Life Plan (2005); runs 63rd Street corridor programming.

name: Taylor Electric Company
aliases: Sam Taylor / Taylor Electric Company; Taylor Electric
description: Chicago electrical contracting company founded in 1922 by Sam Taylor -- the first Black-owned construction company in Chicago (IBEW) and the city's oldest continuously operating Black-owned business. Taylor earned his electrician's license in 1922 (perhaps the first issued to an African American by Chicago) after studying a correspondence course a Greek-American friend ordered under his own name. Early work included Motor Row District doorbells and lights; major projects span the Sears Tower, O'Hare Airport, Soldier Field, Navy Pier, and Guaranteed Rate Field. Founded in a wooden shack on the South Side in 1922; fourth-generation descendants Kendra Dinkins (president/CEO) and Karen Michele Dinkins (VP/COO) lead the 100+ employee firm today.

name: Tanya DePass
description: Tanya DePass is a game writer and the founder of I Need Diverse Games, an organization which seeks to better diversify all aspects of gaming. She is also creative director of the Into the Mother Lands tabletop role-playing game, a role and the founding both documented in a 2024 Take This profile, which described the game as upcoming at that time. Her graph record places her work in the 2010s to the present, within CTL's Black technology research.

description: Chicago Black press figure: Thomas “Tom” Picou, former Chicago Defender editor and chairman of Real Times LLC, which acquired Sengstacke Enterprises in 2003; nephew of John Sengstacke.

aliases: Chicago Chapter of The Links; Links Chicago Chapter
description: Chicago (IL) Chapter of The Links, Incorporated, the Black women's volunteer service organization founded nationally in 1946; the chapter dates to circa 1951, and its archives are housed at the Carter G. Woodson Vivian Harsh Collection.

name: The Power Plant
description: The Power Plant was a house-music club at 1015 N. Halsted Street, on Goose Island, founded by Frankie Knuckles in 1983 after he left the Warehouse. The City of Chicago's Warehouse landmark report — one of this record's own sources — verifies the address and the founding: when the Warehouse doubled admission in late 1982 and grew more commercial, Knuckles left and established his own club, and his followers came with him. Knuckles DJed at the Power Plant until 1986, when he returned to New York City and established Def Mix with David Morales. Where the Warehouse had been a largely gay, Black and Latino room, scene accounts describe Knuckles translating the sound to a broader audience at the Power Plant — a characterization CTL's research carries as Provisional, from a single archivist source, and this record keeps that grade visible. The building's fate after Knuckles's 1986 departure is unresolved in CTL's venue research, so this record makes no claim about the site's current status.

name: The Music Box
description: After Frankie Knuckles's 1982 departure from the Warehouse, owner Robert Williams rebranded/reopened the club as the Music Box (1983) at a new location and hired Ron Hardy as resident DJ.

name: The repast
description: The communal meal served after a homegoing service, prepared by church women ('church ladies') — cornbread dressing, baked mac 'n' cheese, casseroles — where the community feeds the bereaved family.

name: The formal 'front room' (living room kept for company)
description: A front or formal living room kept pristine 'for company only' — plastic-covered upholstery, doilies, china cabinet, pressed carpet lines — as a curated presentation of family respectability and aspiration.

name: Traveling with the Negro Motorist Green Book — Chicago as destination
description: Black motorists used the Green Book (1936–1966) to find welcoming hotels, restaurants, gas stations, and attractions; Chicago's listings concentrated ~80% in Bronzeville, effectively mapping the everyday Black commercial landscape for travelers.

name: The kitchenette apartment
description: Subdivided six-room flats carved into single-room units with shared bathrooms — the dominant dwelling technology of Black Chicago's Black Belt, 1920s–1950s.

name: The Black family photograph album
description: The Black family photograph album is the home archive of everyday Black life: mantelpiece portraits, albums, and loose prints kept, displayed, and inherited by grandmothers and families — in CultureTechLens's LIFE-001 research, an object of Chicago homes citywide, spanning 1900 to the present. Photographer and scholar Deborah Willis treats the family album as a 'sacred archive,' arguing that 'the photos our grandmothers kept on their mantels are just as important as the photos in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.' Willis's own origin point came in 1955, when she found Langston Hughes and Roy DeCarava's The Sweet Flypaper of Life — the first book she had ever seen with people who reminded her of her own family — and learned that ordinary Black stories were 'alive and important and to be cherished.' Her recovery scholarship includes Reflections in Black (2000) and The Family of Black America (1996).

name: Transistor radio (Regency TR-1)
description: The Regency TR-1 was the first commercially manufactured transistor radio. Developed by Texas Instruments with the Regency Division of I.D.E.A., it went on sale on October 18, 1954 — the launch of what Smithsonian Magazine calls the portable electronic age. A small, pocket-sized, battery-powered AM set sold for $50, it was marketed on portability, durability, and battery life — 'music on the go' — and it changed listening habits, moving radio from the living room to the pocket. The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History holds an example donated in 1984 by Dr. Willis A. Adcock of Texas Instruments, along with a clear prototype. CultureTechLens's object biography records the limits of the file plainly: no Chicago maker is verified for the TR-1, no contemporary Black-press symbolism for the transistor radio was located, and a Chicago WVON-listening connection is plausible but unverified.

The Loud Speakers Network was co-founded by Chris Morrow and Reggie Ossé and set out, in Morrow's own words, to provide a platform for African-American and people-of-color voices in podcasting — a positioning the CultureTechLens media research records carefully, noting that the network was marketed toward Black audiences but was not Black-founded. name: There's a Riot Goin' On
description: There’s a Riot Goin’ On is the fifth studio album by Sly and the Family Stone, released November 1, 1971 on Epic Records. Where Stand! had been exuberant, Riot is murky and withdrawn: Sly Stone recorded much of it largely alone in Sausalito and Los Angeles, overdubbing parts over a Maestro Rhythm King drum machine — among the earliest hit albums built on one — and retitling the record in answer to Marvin Gaye’s What’s Going On, released six months earlier. Its title track is listed at zero minutes; “I felt there should be no riots,” Stone later explained. The album topped the Billboard pop and soul album charts, its single “Family Affair” reached number one, the RIAA certified it platinum in 2001, the Grammy Hall of Fame inducted it in 1999, and Rolling Stone’s 2020 greatest-albums list ranked it number 82.

name: The In Crowd
description: The In Crowd is a live album by the Ramsey Lewis Trio — pianist Ramsey Lewis, bassist Eldee Young, and drummer Red Holt — recorded May 13–15, 1965, at the Bohemian Caverns nightclub in Washington, D.C., and released that July on the Argo label. Produced by Esmond Edwards, the album centers on the trio's instrumental reading of “The 'In' Crowd,” Billy Page's song that had been a hit for Dobie Gray the year before. The album topped the Billboard R&B chart and reached No. 2 on the Billboard 200, and it was certified gold; the title single reached No. 5 on the Hot 100 and No. 2 on the R&B chart. The album won the Grammy Award for Best Instrumental Jazz Performance — Small Group or Soloist with Small Group, and the title track was nominated for Record of the Year; in 2009 the single entered the Grammy Hall of Fame.

name: Timbaland

description: Timothy Mosley, known as Timbaland, is a record producer, songwriter and rapper from Norfolk, Virginia, whose off-kilter rhythms redrew the sound of R&B and hip-hop in the late 1990s. Starting as a teenage DJ, he broke through in 1996 producing Ginuwine's debut album and most of Aaliyah's One in a Million, then produced Missy Elliott's debut Supa Dupa Fly the following year. His signature style — stuttering drum programming, unusual samples and space left deliberately in the groove — powered hits for Jay-Z, Ludacris and Nelly Furtado, and defined Justin Timberlake's FutureSex/LoveSounds era. As a solo artist he scored hits including "Give It to Me" and "Apologize" with OneRepublic. In 2020 he co-created the Verzuz livestream series with Swizz Beatz, and in 2024 he was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame.

description: Michael Lamar White, known as Trippie Redd, is a rapper and singer from Canton, Ohio, whose genre-blurring music helped define the emo-rap and rage sounds of the streaming era. Raised in Canton and inspired to rap in part by an older brother who died when White was ten, he began posting tracks online as a teenager and broke out with his 2017 mixtape A Love Letter to You and its single "Love Scars." His debut album, Life's a Trip (2018), reached the Billboard 200 top five, and A Love Letter to You 4 (2019) became his first number-one album. Drawing equally on Lil Wayne and T-Pain and on punk and metal acts such as Slipknot and Marilyn Manson, he has sustained a prolific release pace through albums including Pegasus, Trip at Knight and Mansion Musik, and collaborations with XXXTentacion, Travis Scott and Playboi Carti.

name: Tinashe
description: Kentucky-born, Los Angeles-raised singer, dancer and actress who began as a child performer, survived the major-label machine, and rebuilt herself as one of independent R&B's most durable artists. Tinashe Jorgensen Kachingwe was born on February 6, 1993, in Lexington, Kentucky, worked as a child actor and model, and sang in the girl group the Stunners from 2007 until their 2011 split. Recording mixtapes in her home studio, she signed with RCA Records and broke through with the single 2 On (2014), featuring ScHoolboy Q, which topped the Rhythmic airplay chart and peaked at No. 24 on the Billboard Hot 100 ahead of her debut album Aquarius. Nightride (2016) and Joyride (2018) completed her RCA trilogy. Independent, she released Songs for You (2019), 333 (2021), BB/Ang3l (2023) and Quantum Baby (2024), whose single Nasty became her first solo Hot 100 entry in a decade. A 2025 remix of No Broke Boys carried her back to the top 40, and in 2026 she returned to a major label with her eighth album, Popstar, on Atlantic.

name: Travis Scott
aliases: Jacques Bermon Webster II; Jacques Webster II; La Flame
description: Travis Scott, born Jacques Bermon Webster II in Houston, Texas, in 1991, is an American rapper, singer and producer known for heavily produced, atmospheric recordings and large-scale live spectacle. After early mixtapes including Owl Pharaoh and Days Before Rodeo, his debut studio album Rodeo appeared in 2015. Birds in the Trap Sing McKnight, released in 2016, became his first number-one album on the Billboard 200. Astroworld, named for a closed Houston amusement park, followed in 2018 and produced Sicko Mode, his first Billboard Hot 100 number-one single, made with Drake. Through his Cactus Jack imprint he has released collective projects and built a brand extending into fashion and live events. Utopia, released in 2023 after a long gap between studio albums, also debuted at number one. His career also carries a grave public record: a crowd crush during his Astroworld Festival set in Houston on November 5, 2021, killed ten people, an event that prompted wide scrutiny of festival safety and remains part of any honest account of his public life.

name: Tyler, the Creator
aliases: Tyler Gregory Okonma; Tyler Okonma; Wolf Haley
description: Tyler, the Creator, born Tyler Gregory Okonma in California in 1991, is an American rapper, producer, designer and visual artist who emerged as the co-founder and leader of the Los Angeles collective Odd Future. His self-released Bastard in 2009 and Goblin in 2011, driven by the single Yonkers, brought confrontational, horror-influenced early work to a wide young audience. From Wolf onward his writing and production opened toward jazz, soul and R&B, a turn confirmed by the acclaim for Flower Boy in 2017. Igor in 2019 and Call Me If You Get Lost in 2021 both debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and each won the Grammy Award for Best Rap Album. Chromakopia in 2024 also debuted at number one in the United States. Alongside recording, Okonma built the Golf Wang clothing line, the luxury label Golf le Fleur and the Camp Flog Gnaw Carnival festival, making design and world-building a continuous part of the music rather than merchandise added afterward.

name: Tim Scott
description: Timothy Eugene Scott (born September 19, 1965, in North Charleston, South Carolina) is the United States senator from South Carolina and, in the Senate that has sat since January 2025, the only Black Republican in the chamber. He climbed the ladder rung by rung: Charleston County Council from 1995 to 2009, the South Carolina House from 2009 to 2011, and the U.S. House of Representatives from 2011 until January 2, 2013, when Governor Nikki Haley appointed him to the Senate seat vacated by Jim DeMint's resignation. He then won the 2014 special election and full terms in 2016 and 2022. Scott is the first Black senator from South Carolina — a state that sent Black representatives to the House during Reconstruction but had never sent a Black senator to Washington — and the first Black American to serve in both the House and the Senate. In May 2023 he launched a campaign for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination, suspending it that November. With Booker, Warnock, Blunt Rochester, and Alsobrooks, he completes the five — the largest number of Black senators ever to serve simultaneously.

name: The Bernie Mac Show
description: The Bernie Mac Show, created by Larry Wilmore and built on the stand-up of the Chicago comedian Bernie Mac, aired on Fox from November 14, 2001, to April 14, 2006 — five seasons in which Mac, playing a version of himself, took in his sister's three children and narrated the collision between his old-school discipline and their needs directly to the camera ('America,' as he addressed the audience). The form was the break: single-camera, no laugh track, confession-to-lens — a stand-up's aside rebuilt as a sitcom's architecture, formally distinct from the multi-camera Black family comedies that preceded it. The industry ratified it at the top level: a Peabody Award in its first season and an Emmy for Outstanding Writing for a Comedy Series. The NAACP Image Awards named it Outstanding Comedy Series three times, and Mac himself won the Image Award for Outstanding Actor in a Comedy Series four consecutive years, 2003 through 2006, alongside a Television Critics Association individual achievement honor. The graph files it as the bridge between the Fox bloc of the nineties and the single-camera Black sitcoms of the next decade.

name: The Color Purple (1985 film)
description: The Color Purple, directed by Steven Spielberg with a score and co-production by Quincy Jones and adapted from Alice Walker's 1982 Pulitzer Prize-winning novel, was released by Warner Bros. on December 18, 1985, following Celie — played by Whoopi Goldberg in her breakthrough role — across decades of rural Georgia toward her own voice. It stands in awards history by an anomaly: nominated for eleven Academy Awards, including Best Picture, it won none, tying the record for the most nominations without a win, with Spielberg's absence from the directing slate the standing oddity inside the record. Goldberg won the Golden Globe for Best Actress in a Drama, and the film was the screen debut of Oprah Winfrey, Oscar-nominated in support. It was also a major commercial success, though the precise worldwide gross is reported inconsistently across sources and is left unstated here rather than blended. The graph files the film beside Walker's novel as the 1980s' central Black literary adaptation — a work whose shutout the culture has spent forty years treating as the Academy's error, not the film's.

name: Tan Confessions
description: Tan Confessions was a monthly true-confessions magazine for Black women readers, launched in Chicago in November 1950 by the Johnson Publishing Company, five years after Ebony and a year before Jet. Built on reader-submitted confessions, it mixed its three main departments — 'Stories from True Life,' 'Special Features,' and a 'Home Service Magazine' of homemaking, beauty, child care, and health — with letters and advice columns, selling at twenty-five cents a copy. Ben Burns, Ebony's founding editor, served as its executive editor, and John H. Johnson reported that it quickly reached a circulation of some 300,000. The title was shortened to Tan in September 1952, renamed Black Stars in November 1971, and discontinued in July 1981, a thirty-one-year run that made it one of Johnson Publishing's longest-lived secondary titles and a rare archive of Black women's interior lives in the 1950s.

name: Tim Hardaway Sr.
description: Timothy Duane Hardaway Sr. (born September 1, 1966, in Chicago) is the Chicago-born point guard whose “UTEP two-step” crossover became one of the defining moves in basketball. He starred at Chicago's Carver High School, which retired his jersey in 2022, and at UTEP under coach Don Haskins, where he won the 1989 Frances Pomeroy Naismith Award and WAC Player of the Year honors. Drafted 14th overall by the Golden State Warriors in 1989, he formed the Run TMC trio with Chris Mullin and Mitch Richmond, then led the Miami Heat through their late-1990s peak — five All-Star selections, the 1997 All-NBA First Team, and Olympic gold at Sydney in 2000. He finished his playing career with 15,373 points and 7,095 assists, later served as a Detroit Pistons assistant coach from 2014 to 2018, and was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2022. He is the father of NBA guard Tim Hardaway Jr.

name: The Ramsey Lewis Trio
description: The Ramsey Lewis Trio was the Chicago jazz piano trio led by Ramsey Lewis (1935–2022) with bassist Eldee Young and drummer Isaac “Redd” Holt. Formed in Chicago in 1956, the group signed to Chess Records and debuted that year with Ramsey Lewis and His Gentle-men of Swing. After nearly a decade of straight-ahead jazz, the trio recorded Dobie Gray's song “The In Crowd” in 1965; the single reached No. 5 on the Billboard Hot 100, the album reached No. 2, and the recording won the Grammy Award for Best Jazz Performance. Follow-up hits “Hang On Sloopy” and “Wade in the Water” made the trio one of the most commercially successful jazz groups of the 1960s. Young and Holt left in 1966 to form Young-Holt Unlimited and were replaced by Cleveland Eaton and Maurice White; the three founders reunited for the 1983 album Reunion.

name: Thundercat
description: Thundercat (born Stephen Lee Bruner, October 19, 1984, in Los Angeles, California) is an American bassist, singer, and producer. He first came to prominence as a teenage member of the crossover thrash band Suicidal Tendencies before becoming a central figure in Los Angeles's jazz-funk underground and the West Coast Get Down collective. His bass work anchors Kendrick Lamar's To Pimp a Butterfly (2015), and he won the Grammy Award for Best Rap/Sung Performance for the track “These Walls.” On Flying Lotus's Brainfeeder label he released The Golden Age of Apocalypse (2011), Apocalypse (2013), Drunk (2017), and It Is What It Is (2020), the last of which won the Grammy Award for Best Progressive R&B Album. Rolling Stone has ranked him among the greatest bass players of all time. Distracted, the subject of CTL Short #50, is his fifth solo album (2026).

name: The Occidental Book of the Dead
description: The Occidental Book of the Dead is a novel by T. Geronimo Johnson, published by William Morrow on October 6, 2026 — his first novel in eleven years. Johnson, born and raised in the American South, is the author of Hold It 'Til It Hurts (2012), a finalist for the PEN/Faulkner Award, and Welcome to Braggsville (2015), longlisted for the National Book Award and the Andrew Carnegie Medal for Excellence; he won the inaugural Joyce Carol Oates Prize, the Rome Prize, the Ernest J. Gaines Award for Literary Excellence and the William Saroyan International Prize. The new novel follows George Washington Jonson, a Black Atlanta police officer, across two decades after a patrol shooting cracks open the life he has built, in a formally split structure the publisher describes as an exploration of corruption and conspiracy in a divided nation. The National Book Foundation featured Johnson in its fall 2026 NBF Presents season. CultureTechLens covered the book in Short #136, published October 14, 2026.

name: TYSON (2026 documentary series)
description: TYSON is a four-part Netflix documentary series directed by Floyd Russ that premiered on October 13, 2026, built around Mike Tyson accounting for his own life on camera. Its four episodes — 'Power,' 'Greed,' 'Trust' and 'Human' — trace the boxer's path from a chaotic Brooklyn childhood to the youngest heavyweight championship in history, and through the fame, incarceration, financial collapse and reinvention that followed, in what Netflix describes as an unflinching look at one of the most polarizing figures in sports history. The series runs about four hours and twenty-three minutes in total. Executive producers include Bill Simmons, Jim Gray and Ian Orefice; Tyson participated on camera but is not an executive producer. CultureTechLens covered the premiere in Short #138, published October 14, 2026. Mike Tyson himself has no record in this graph yet — he is named in this packet as a further gap.

name: The Greatest
description: The Greatest is an eight-episode Prime Video limited series — the first authorized scripted series about Muhammad Ali — created and showrun by Ben Watkins, premiering all episodes on November 4, 2026, in more than 240 countries and territories. Jaalen Best stars as the young Cassius Clay becoming Muhammad Ali, with Omari Hardwick as Cassius Clay Sr., Dana Gourrier as Odessa 'Bird' Clay, Kai Parham as Rudy Clay, Amin Joseph as Sonny Liston, Giovanni Ribisi as trainer Angelo Dundee and Michael Ealy as Malcolm X. The production, from Amazon MGM Studios with Michael B. Jordan's Outlier Society and Roc Nation among its partners, carries the participation of the Ali estate: the boxer's widow, Lonnie Ali, is an executive producer. Prime Video released the official trailer on October 14, 2026. CultureTechLens covered the series in Short #151, published October 14, 2026. Muhammad Ali himself has no record in this graph yet — he is named in this packet as a further gap.

name: Tonya Lewis Lee
description: Tonya Lewis Lee, born Tonya Linnette Lewis on March 30, 1966, in Yonkers, New York, is an American attorney, producer, author, and women's-health advocate. She earned a bachelor's degree from Sarah Lawrence College in 1988 and a law degree from the University of Virginia School of Law in 1991, then practiced corporate and First Amendment law in Washington, D.C. She married filmmaker Spike Lee in 1993 and founded the production company Madstone Company Inc. in 1998, producing children's and documentary programming for Nickelodeon and others, including the miniseries Miracle's Boys and the Brown v. Board of Education documentary I Sit Where I Want (2004). With Nikki Silver she co-founded ToniK Productions, which produced The Watsons Go to Birmingham from her own screenplay. She co-authored three children's books with Spike Lee and the novel Gotham Diaries, served as spokesperson for the federal “A Healthy Baby Begins With You” infant-mortality campaign, and directed the maternal-health documentary Aftershock (2022), which won a Peabody Award.

name: Trina
description: Trina (born Katrina Laverne Taylor in Miami, Florida — her birth year is reported variously as 1974 and 1975) is Miami's defining female MC, the Southern counterweight to the explicit style Lil' Kim had blown up from Brooklyn. A Liberty City native studying for a real-estate career, she had no musical ambition when Trick Daddy recruited her for "Nann" (1998), which reached number three on Billboard's rap chart. Her debut Da Baddest Bitch (2000) was certified gold within eight months, and she followed it with a run of top-twenty albums — Diamond Princess (2002), Glamorest Life (2005), Still da Baddest (2008) and Amazin' (2010). She led the film A Miami Tail (2003), the role the CTL Short bills, later starred on Love & Hip Hop: Miami, received BET's I Am Hip Hop Award in 2022, and published her memoir Da Baddest in 2024. name: Teyana Taylor
description: Teyana Taylor (born December 10, 1990, in Harlem, New York) is the singer, dancer and actress whose career ran from a teenage Star Trak signing to a Golden Globe. Signed to Pharrell Williams's Star Trak at fifteen and introduced on MTV's My Super Sweet Sixteen (2007), she sang on Kanye West's My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy (2010) and joined his GOOD Music label in 2012. Her debut album VII (2014) topped Billboard's Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart, and her performance in West's "Fade" video, premiered at the 2016 MTV Video Music Awards, became a cultural flashpoint. After K.T.S.E. (2018) — certified gold by the RIAA in June 2025 — she announced a retirement from music in 2020 and pivoted to acting, winning the National Board of Review's Breakthrough Performance award for A Thousand and One (2023) and the Golden Globe for Best Supporting Actress for One Battle After Another (2025). name: The Last Poets
description: The Last Poets are the Harlem poetry collective whose percussion-backed spoken word, first performed in 1968, is documented as a groundwork layer of hip-hop. The original group — Gylan Kain, David Nelson and Abiodun Oyewole — formed on May 19, 1968, Malcolm X's birthday, at Mount Morris Park (now Marcus Garvey Park) in East Harlem, taking their name from a poem by the South African writer Keorapetse Kgositsile, who had written of living in the age of the gun, when poetry's era had ended and the last poets were at hand. The best-known lineup — Jalal Mansur Nuriddin, Umar Bin Hassan and Oyewole, with percussionist Nilaja Obabi — appeared on the television program Soul! in 1969 and released the self-titled debut album The Last Poets in 1970 and This Is Madness in 1971, records that joined Black nationalist politics to chant, rhythm and jazz. AllMusic's Jason Ankeny wrote that the group almost single-handedly laid the groundwork for hip-hop's emergence. Later lineups recorded into the 2010s, including Understand What Black Is (2018); Nuriddin died in 2018. CultureTechLens profiled the group in Short #187.

name: The Volume
description: The Volume is the sports media company and podcast network founded by broadcaster Colin Cowherd and launched on February 1, 2021, with iHeartMedia as its advertising sales partner. Built around Cowherd's own program and a roster of athlete- and creator-led shows — among them The Draymond Green Show — the network reported 1.2 million subscribers and a combined 40 million podcast downloads per month in 2022, and in September 2023 it signed DraftKings as the presenting sponsor of its podcast and video content. Its catalog includes, since May 2025, Joe and Jada, the podcast hosted by Fat Joe and Jadakiss and billed jointly by iHeartPodcasts and The Volume. Front Office Sports has reported investor interest in the company, which Cowherd has said he values above $100 million — a founder's figure, carried here as reported.

name: Tory Lanez
aliases: Daystar Peterson; Daystar Shemuel Shua Peterson
description: Tory Lanez, born Daystar Peterson on 27 July 1992 in Brampton, Ontario, Canada, is a Canadian rapper and singer. After early support from Sean Kingston, he signed an Interscope-affiliated Mad Love deal in 2015 and broke through with "Say It," which peaked at No. 23 on the Hot 100 and went multi-platinum. His debut album I Told You (2016) was followed by Memories Don't Die (2018), No. 1 in Canada, and by Chixtape 5 (2019) and The New Toronto 3 (2020), both No. 2 in the US; his single "Luv" was Grammy-nominated for Best R&B Song. In December 2022 he was convicted on three felony firearm counts in the 2020 shooting of Megan Pete (Megan Thee Stallion), and in August 2023 he was sentenced to ten years in California state prison, per the Los Angeles County District Attorney.

name: That Girl Lay Lay
description: That Girl Lay Lay, born Alaya High on 28 January 2007 in Houston, Texas, is an American rapper and actress. She began posting rap videos on YouTube at age six, and her freestyle videos — notably over BlocBoy JB's "Shoot" — built her following. At eleven she was reported as the youngest female African American rapper signed to a major record deal, with Empire Distribution; her debut single "Go, Lay Lay, Go" and debut album Tha Cheat Code followed in 2018. Nickelodeon signed her to an overall deal in 2020, and she starred as Lay Lay in the sitcom That Girl Lay Lay (premiered 23 September 2021; ended 20 March 2024). She has a book series with Scholastic and a voice credit in Vampirina: Teenage Vampire in an episode aired 19 September 2025. name: Tay Keith
description: Tay Keith, born Brytavious Lakeith Chambers on 20 September 1996 in Memphis, Tennessee, was an American record producer who defined the Memphis trap sound of the late 2010s. He began making beats at about fourteen, posting to YouTube and DatPiff, and built a long partnership with fellow Memphian BlocBoy JB. He produced BlocBoy JB's "Look Alive" featuring Drake and Drake's "Nonstop" in 2018 and co-produced Travis Scott's "Sicko Mode"; he also produced Beyoncé's "Before I Let Go" for Homecoming. He graduated from Middle Tennessee State University in December 2018 and founded the Nashville label and studio Drumatized. He was found dead in his Nashville apartment on 18 June 2026, aged 29, during a police welfare check; Tennessee officials later confirmed an accidental drug overdose as the cause.

name: The Lox
description: The Lox is an American hip-hop trio from Yonkers, New York, composed of Jadakiss, Styles P and Sheek Louch. The three rapped together in high school under the names the Bomb Squad and then the Warlocks; a demo recorded with Jaz-O reached fellow Yonkers native Mary J. Blige and then Sean Combs, who signed the group to Bad Boy Records and shortened its name to the Lox, later read as Living Off Experience. After featured work in 1997, including 'We'll Always Love Big Poppa' and the remix of 'All About the Benjamins,' the group released its Top Ten debut album, Money, Power & Respect (1998). Dissatisfied at Bad Boy, the trio moved to Ruff Ryders Entertainment in 1999 and released We Are the Streets (2000), another Top Ten album. Each member then built a solo career, making the Lox one of the few groups with a Top Ten Billboard 200 entry from every member. The group later resumed recording together through its own D-Block label, releasing Filthy America... It's Beautiful (2016) and Living Off Xperience (2020). Jadakiss holds a record in this graph (CTL-E-5704); Styles P and Sheek Louch do not yet, and are documented as further gaps rather than minted here.

name: Terror Squad
description: Terror Squad is an American hip-hop collective from the Bronx, New York, established in 1998, with Fat Joe among its founding members. The crew — Fat Joe, Big Pun, Cuban Link, Prospect, Armageddon and Triple Seis, with singer Tony Sunshine — debuted as a group on Fat Joe's album Don Cartagena (1998), coming together on the track 'The Hidden Hand,' and released its self-titled debut album on Atlantic in September 1999, which produced no substantial hits. The group went on hiatus after Big Pun's death in 2000; Cuban Link and Triple Seis departed, and Remy Ma and Tony Sunshine became central to the regrouped lineup. Terror Squad reunited for its second album, True Story (2004), whose single 'Lean Back,' produced by Scott Storch and performed by Fat Joe and Remy Ma, peaked at number one on the Billboard Hot 100. The collective signed to Koch Records in 2007, and Remy Ma parted ways with the group that April. Fat Joe, the member with the most successful solo career, holds a record in this graph (CTL-E-5703); Big Pun does not, and his member edge is documented as a further gap rather than minted here.

name: Tito Jackson
aliases: Toriano Adaryll Jackson; Tariano Adaryll Jackson
description: Tito Jackson, born 15 October 1953 in Gary, Indiana, was an American musician, singer and songwriter, a founding member of the Jackson 5 and the group's guitarist and background vocalist. One of the Jackson family's children raised in Gary, he formed the group with his brothers Jackie, Jermaine, Marlon and Michael; signed to Motown in 1969, the Jackson 5 became the first group whose first four singles — "I Want You Back," "ABC," "The Love You Save" and "I'll Be There" — all reached No. 1. After the group left Motown it continued as the Jacksons on Epic Records, and Tito remained one of its most consistent members across its full history. The Jackson 5 were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1997. Tito began a solo career as a blues musician in 2003 and released the solo albums Tito Time (2016) and Under Your Spell (2021). He was still performing with Jackie and Marlon as the Jacksons in the summer of 2024. He died on 15 September 2024 in Gallup, New Mexico, at age 70.

name: Terry Crews
description: Terry Crews, born Terry Alan Crews on 30 July 1968 in Flint, Michigan, is an American actor, television host and former professional football player who built two full careers in public. A defensive end and linebacker at Western Michigan University, he was drafted by the Los Angeles Rams in the eleventh round of the 1991 NFL Draft and played in the NFL for the Rams, the San Diego Chargers and Washington, with a World League of American Football season for the Rhein Fire in Germany; Pro Football Reference credits him with 32 games played. After football he rebuilt himself as an actor: Julius Rock, the frugal father of Everybody Hates Chris (2005–2009), made him a sitcom fixture, and Sergeant, later Lieutenant, Terry Jeffords on Brooklyn Nine-Nine (2013–2021) made him a beloved one. His film work runs from Friday After Next (2002) and White Chicks (2004) to The Expendables series. Since 2019 he has hosted NBC's America's Got Talent. He was among the group named Time Person of the Year in 2017, the 'Silence Breakers,' after speaking publicly about sexual assault, and he has spoken openly about the abuse his family endured during his Flint childhood.

name: Tri-State Defender
description: The Tri-State Defender is a weekly African-American newspaper published in Memphis, Tennessee, serving Memphis and nearby areas of Arkansas, Mississippi, and Tennessee — the three states of its name. It was founded in 1951 by John H. Sengstacke, owner of the Chicago Defender, who saw Memphis as a market where Black newspapers had repeatedly failed to take root; Sengstacke and editor Lewis O. Swingler, formerly of the rival Memphis World, published the first edition in November 1951, a 20-page issue carrying a ten-point program, and Swingler served as editor in chief until 1955. The paper became part of Sengstacke's newspaper chain alongside the Chicago Defender, the Michigan Chronicle, and later the Pittsburgh Courier, and billed itself as the Mid-South's alternative newspaper. In 2013 it was purchased locally from Real Times Media by the Tri-State Defender Board of Directors, and it continues publishing from Memphis.

name: Tamron Hall
description: Tamron Hall, born September 16, 1970, in Luling, Texas, is an American broadcast journalist, television talk show host, and author. She was raised in Luling, where her mother was an educator, and earned a Bachelor of Arts in Broadcast Journalism from Temple University in 1992. She began her career at KBTX-TV in Bryan, Texas, then worked at KTVT in Fort Worth before spending a decade in Chicago television: from 1997 to 2007 she worked for WFLD in Chicago as a general assignment reporter, consumer reporter, and host of the three-hour Fox News in the Morning, frequently reporting on Chicago politics and breaking news. In July 2007 she joined MSNBC and NBC News, where she became a national news correspondent, hosted MSNBC Live with Tamron Hall, and co-hosted Today's Take, the third hour of Today, from 2014 to 2017; USA Today reports that she became the first Black woman to co-anchor the Today show. She also hosts Deadline: Crime on Investigation Discovery. In September 2019 she debuted her self-titled syndicated daytime talk show, Tamron Hall, which has earned her two Daytime Emmy Awards. USA Today reported in September 2026 that the show had reached its eighth season.

name: Tristan Thompson
description: Tristan Thompson, born Tristan Trevor James Thompson on 13 March 1991 in Brampton, Ontario, Canada, is a Canadian-American former center and one of the most successful Canadian players of his generation, raised by parents of Jamaican descent. After one season at the University of Texas, where he was Big 12 Freshman of the Year, Cleveland selected him fourth overall in the 2011 NBA draft — at the time the highest a Canadian had ever been picked. He made the NBA All-Rookie Second Team and became the Cavaliers' durable interior anchor, twice leading the league in games played. Starting all 21 playoff games, he helped Cleveland win the 2016 NBA championship, the first in franchise history, coming back from a 3-1 Finals deficit against Golden State. He later played for Boston, Sacramento, Indiana, Chicago and the Los Angeles Lakers before returning to Cleveland for 2023-25. Across 819 regular-season games he averaged 8.3 points and 7.8 rebounds. Unsigned through 2025-26, he confirmed his retirement as a player in 2026 and took a global ambassador role with Dubai Basketball.

name: Tyrese Haliburton
description: Tyrese Haliburton, born Tyrese John Haliburton on 29 February 2000 in Oshkosh, Wisconsin, is an American point guard for the Indiana Pacers. The son of John Haliburton, a referee and former women's coach, and Brenda Haliburton, he starred at Oshkosh North High School and then at Iowa State, where he set the program's single-game assists record and made the All-Big 12 second team as a sophomore. Sacramento selected him 12th overall in the 2020 NBA draft, and in February 2022 Indiana acquired him in the trade centered on Domantas Sabonis. In Indiana he became a two-time All-Star (2023, as a reserve, and 2024, as a starter) and a two-time All-NBA Third Team selection, and in 2025 he led the Pacers to their first NBA Finals appearance in 25 years. He won Olympic gold with the United States at Paris 2024. In Game 7 of the 2025 Finals he tore his right Achilles tendon and missed the entire 2025-26 season. After sixteen months of rehabilitation he returned in the October 2026 preseason, scoring 24 points in 18 minutes at Oklahoma City on his second game back.

name: Tha Carter III
description: Tha Carter III is the sixth studio album by Lil Wayne, released June 10, 2008, on Cash Money, Universal Motown, and Young Money. It debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 with 1,005,545 copies sold in its first week and reached 2.88 million copies by the end of 2008. Its singles — “Lollipop,” which held number one on the Hot 100 for five weeks, “A Milli,” “Got Money,” and “Mrs. Officer” — made Wayne the dominant popular musician of his moment; guests include Jay-Z, T-Pain, Kanye West, Babyface, and Robin Thicke, and “Lollipop” carries a credited posthumous appearance by Static Major, who died in February 2008. At the 2009 Grammy Awards the album was nominated for Album of the Year and won Best Rap Album, while “Lollipop” won Best Rap Song and “A Milli” won Best Rap Solo Performance. Rolling Stone placed the album on its 500 Greatest Albums list.

name: Tyreek Hill
description: Tyreek Hill, born 1 March 1994 in Douglas, Georgia, is an American professional football wide receiver, nicknamed 'Cheetah' for his speed. Drafted by the Kansas City Chiefs in the fifth round in 2016, he made the Pro Bowl as a rookie returner and receiver and helped Kansas City win Super Bowl LIV after the 2019 season. In six seasons with the Chiefs he became one of the league's most feared deep threats. Traded to the Miami Dolphins in 2022, he produced consecutive 1,700-yard receiving seasons — 1,710 yards in 2022 and a franchise-record 1,799 yards with 13 touchdowns in 2023, when he led the NFL in receiving yards and was ranked first on the NFL Top 100. A dislocated left knee with multiple ligament tears in September 2025 ended his season after four games; Miami released him in February 2026, and in October 2026 he remained a free agent rehabilitating the knee while his agent discussed a return with multiple teams.

name: Terence Crawford
description: Terence Crawford (born Terence Allan Crawford on 28 September 1987 in Omaha, Nebraska) is an American former professional boxer who retired undefeated as the defining fighter of his generation. Fighting out of Omaha, which he represented throughout his career, he turned professional in 2008 and won world championships in five weight classes, from lightweight to super middleweight. He became undisputed champion at light welterweight in 2017 and at welterweight in 2023, when he stopped Errol Spence Jr., and in August 2024 he added a super welterweight title. On 13 September 2025, before 70,482 fans at Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas, he rose two further divisions and outpointed Canelo Álvarez by unanimous decision to take the undisputed super middleweight championship, becoming the first male boxer of the four-belt era to be undisputed in three divisions. On 16 December 2025 he announced his retirement, closing his career at 42 wins, no losses, 31 by knockout, with his final twenty bouts all contested with a title on the line. Through 2026 he remained retired despite public calls for a Canelo rematch.

name: T-Bone Walker
aliases: Aaron Thibeaux Walker; Oak Cliff T-Bone
description: Aaron Thibeaux 'T-Bone' Walker (May 28, 1910 – March 16, 1975) was the first important electric-guitar soloist in the blues and one of the most influential guitarists in the idiom's history. Born in Linden, Texas, and raised in Dallas by musical parents, he guided the blind singer Blind Lemon Jefferson around the city as a boy, first recorded as Oak Cliff T-Bone in 1929, and befriended the young Charlie Christian. Settling in California in 1934, he developed a fluent single-note electric style, phrasing horn-like lines with swinging ease behind his own smooth singing. His 1947 recording 'Call It Stormy Monday' became an enduring blues standard, followed by records such as 'T-Bone Shuffle' and 'Bobby Sox Blues.' Singers and guitarists from B.B. King to Chuck Berry studied him, and his stagecraft — playing behind his back and with his teeth — entered the rock vocabulary. His album Good Feelin' won a Grammy Award, and he was inducted into the Blues Hall of Fame in 1980 and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1987.

name: T. Thomas Fortune
description: Timothy Thomas Fortune (1856–1928) was born enslaved in Marianna, Florida, and became the leading Black newspaper editor of his generation. His father Emanuel, a Reconstruction-era Florida legislator, secured him work as a legislative page, where he learned politics and the printer's trade; he later studied briefly at Howard University and worked in the print shop of the People's Advocate in Washington. Moving to New York around 1880, Fortune took over the Rumor and renamed it the New York Globe, then launched the Freeman, the paper that became the New York Age in 1887 — the Black weekly he edited, with interruptions, for two decades. His editorials attacked segregation, lynching, the convict lease system, and both political parties when they abandoned Black voters, and argued that Black Americans should defend themselves if attacked. In 1884 he published Black and White: Land, Labor, and Politics in the South, and he helped found the National Afro-American League, an early national civil rights organization whose model later fed the Niagara Movement and the NAACP. He ended his career editing Marcus Garvey's Negro World from 1923 until his death in Philadelphia in 1928, eulogized as the dean of Black journalists.

name: Theatre Owners Booking Association
aliases: Theater Owners Booking Association; TOBA; T.O.B.A.
description: The Theatre Owners Booking Association, known everywhere as TOBA, was formed in the early 1920s to book Black entertainers into a circuit of theaters serving Black audiences under segregation. Its governing board was interracial, many of its agents and theater owners were Black, and it gave performers a shareholder-linked route to steady work at a time when white vaudeville circuits largely excluded them. Through TOBA's books passed Josephine Baker, Cab Calloway, Ethel Waters, Ma Rainey, and Bessie Smith, and the circuit nurtured tap dancers including Leonard Reed and Willie Bryant and the Whitman Sisters. Performers also knew its other name for the initials, Tough on Black Artists, for grueling routes and demanding terms. TOBA grew so dominant that Sherman Dudley, the Black entrepreneur who had built a rival circuit from 1911, merged his theaters into it. By the early 1930s the association had collapsed, hastened by the Great Depression and financial mismanagement, leaving a vacuum that later Black booking agencies, above all the Ferguson brothers in Indianapolis, would fill within the wider chitlin' circuit.

name: Tatyana Guchi
description: Tatyana Guchi — born Tatyana Komaguchi — is a Los Angeles-based stand-up comedian, actress, improviser and musician whose official biography describes her point of view as shaped by 'the Black, Queer, and Asian perspective.' Raised with East Coast and Southern roots, she came up through Los Angeles stand-up and improv rather than television: she was named a Laugh Factory Fresh Face, was a finalist for Breakout Comedian of the Year at the American Black Film Festival's Because They're Funny comedy festival, has been heard on SiriusXM's Netflix Is a Joke Radio, and has recorded sets for Cracked Comedy and for the Newcomers showcase on Veeps. She is creative director of the improv group BMC Improv (formerly Bernie Mac & Cheese) and teaches improv at the Terasaki Budokan Japanese community center in downtown Los Angeles, and she has appeared in commercials for Old Navy, Sephora and Android. In October 2026 she was named to the cast of the sketch-comedy channel Smosh, joining its ensemble after appearing as a 'friend of' the channel.

name: Tiffany Haddish
description: Tiffany Haddish, born 3 December 1979 in South Central Los Angeles, is an American stand-up comedian and actress. Her father, Tsihaye Reda Haddish, was a refugee from Eritrea; her mother, Leola, was an African American business owner. After her mother suffered severe brain damage in a car accident, Haddish entered foster care at twelve and found her footing at a Laugh Factory comedy camp. Years of small roles and stand-up led to a star-making turn as Dina in Girls Trip (2017), named among the century's best film performances by The New Yorker. That year she became the first Black woman stand-up comedian to host Saturday Night Live, winning a Primetime Emmy for the episode, and published the best-selling memoir The Last Black Unicorn. Her album Black Mitzvah (2019) won the Grammy Award for Best Comedy Album in 2021. In 2019 she became a naturalized Eritrean citizen while burying her father in his homeland, and she has publicly honored her Eritrean heritage throughout her career.

name: Tracy Morgan
description: Tracy Morgan, born November 10, 1968, in New York City and raised in Brooklyn's Marlboro and Tompkins Houses in Bedford-Stuyvesant, is an American stand-up comedian and actor. After early work as Hustle Man on Martin and on Harlem's Uptown Comedy Club, he joined Saturday Night Live in 1996 and performed as a regular until 2003, creating characters including Brian Fellow and Astronaut Jones. From 2006 to 2013 he played Tracy Jordan, a caricature of himself, on NBC's 30 Rock, earning a Primetime Emmy nomination for Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Comedy Series in 2009. He published the autobiography I Am the New Black in 2009 and later starred as Tray Barker in The Last O.G. from 2018 to 2021. On June 7, 2014, he was critically injured on the New Jersey Turnpike when a Walmart tractor-trailer struck his limousine bus, suffering a traumatic brain injury, a broken femur, a broken nose, and broken ribs; his friend and collaborator James McNair was killed. Morgan settled his lawsuit against Walmart in 2015 and returned to host Saturday Night Live that October.

name: Tesehki
aliases: Latifa Malone; Latifa Tesehki Malone; Sehki
description: Latifa Malone, known as Tesehki, born 22 May 1995 in Baltimore, Maryland, is an American reality television personality and R&B singer. She is the older sister of rapper and television personality Chrisean Rock, one of twelve Malone siblings raised in West Baltimore. She first appeared on Zeus Network's Blueface & Chrisean: Crazy in Love in 2022, then joined the Baddies franchise through the Baddies East auditions and became a cast member of Baddies East in 2023. She returned for Baddies Caribbean in 2024 and Baddies Midwest, which premiered on 3 November 2024, and was a main cast member of Baddies USA, the franchise's eighth season. As a singer she is known for singles including Real As Me, I Need Love and Thinking Bout You. In 2026 The Shade Room reported her among the cast announced for NowThatsTV's Girls Will Be Girls: Act 1.

name: Tyra Banks
description: Tyra Banks, born Tyra Lynne Banks on 4 December 1973 in Inglewood, California, is an American model, television host, producer and businessperson. She began modeling at fifteen, signed with Elite Model Management in 1990 and walked twenty-five shows in her first Paris season. In February 1996 she became the first African American woman featured on the cover of GQ, and she also appeared on the Sports Illustrated swimsuit issue cover and the Victoria's Secret catalog, becoming one of the original Victoria's Secret Angels in 1997. She founded her production company, Bankable Productions, and in 2003 created America's Next Top Model, which she hosted in 2003–15 and again in 2017–18 across the series' twenty-four cycles. Her daytime series The Tyra Banks Show ran from 2005 to 2010 and won Emmy Awards in 2008 and 2009. She later hosted America's Got Talent in 2017–18 and Dancing with the Stars in 2020–22, and she is the founder of the ice-cream brand SMiZE & DREAM, which she now operates from Sydney, Australia.

name: Turkey Stearnes
description: Norman Thomas "Turkey" Stearnes was a five-tool center fielder and one of the Negro leagues' greatest hitters. Born May 8, 1901, in Nashville, Tennessee, he left school after his father's death to help support his family, played professionally in Montgomery in 1921, and joined the Detroit Stars in 1923, becoming the face of that franchise. A left-handed hitter with an unorthodox stance, he combined power, speed, and range, led the Negro National League in batting average twice, and was a five-time East-West All-Star selection. He won pennants with the Chicago American Giants in 1932 and 1933, played for the Kansas City Monarchs from 1938 through 1940, and made a final playing appearance in 1945. Off the field he was quiet and unassuming, and he worked in Detroit industry from 1938 to 1964, by his own account as recorded by SABR. Stearnes died September 4, 1979, in Detroit and was posthumously elected to the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 2000.

name: Teryn Payne
description: Teryn Payne is a journalist-turned-public-relations specialist on Chance the Rapper's executive team at CTR (Chance the Rapper) LLC, per Vocalo/WBEZ, which recounts her bachelor's and master's degrees in journalism from the University of Illinois, a first job at EBONY Magazine as assistant to the editor-in-chief, later work as a Teen Vogue editor and freelance beauty writer for Allure, Glamour and Refinery29, and her 2019 return to Chicago; 2025 Chance the Rapper video credits list her under CTR Management. WVON's roster additionally credits her as CMO of The Retro Grill, the South Side Chicago restaurant; that title is roster-only in this pass. She was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.

name: Troy Vivrett
description: Troy Vivrett is co-founder and Chief Operating Officer of Southern Chicago, the modern, upscale Southern restaurant in Chicago's South Loop (2000 S. Wabash Ave.) serving contemporary Southern brunch, cocktails and dinner in a 6,700-square-foot space with a 140-seat patio and private event space. FSR Magazine describes the independent concept as created and owned by Vivrett and executive chef Xavier Vance. He was named to WVON's 40 Under 40 Game Changers Class of 2026.
